The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Work over ZF. The **real dominated-extension principle**, denoted **HB**, is the following assertion:

For every real vector space $X$, every sublinear functional $p:X\to\mathbb R$ in the sense of [[def-sublinear-functional]], every real linear subspace $M\le X$ in the sense of [[def-linear-subspace]], and every real linear functional $g:M\to\mathbb R$ in the sense of [[def-algebraic-dual-and-linear-functional]],
$$\bigl(\forall m\in M,\ g(m)\le p(m)\bigr)\ \Longrightarrow\ \exists F:X\to\mathbb R\ \bigl(F\text{ is real linear},\ F|_M=g,\ \forall x\in X,\ F(x)\le p(x)\bigr).$$

This names an additional principle; it does not assert a proof of HB in ZF. Subsequent results explicitly state when they assume HB. Neither topology nor completeness is part of this assertion. The subspace may be $\{0\}$ or all of $X$. Sublinearity at scalar zero gives $p(0)=0$, and a linear functional has value zero at zero.

derivations.claim: For each integer $m\ge1$, tightness and [A1] give a compact set $K_m\subset B$ with $\mu(K_m)>1-2^{-m}$. Each compact metric space $K_m$ has a countable dense subset: for each integer $r\ge1$, compactness gives a finite $1/r$-net, and the union of these finite nets is countable and dense. The union over $m$ of these dense subsets is countable; let $S$ be its closure. Then $S$ is separable, contains every $K_m$, and $\mu(S)\ge\mu(K_m)>1-2^{-m}$ for every $m$, hence $\mu(S)=1$.

Let $E$ be the closed real linear span of $S$. Rational linear combinations of a countable dense subset of $S$ form a countable dense subset of its real linear span, so $E$ is separable; it is closed by construction and therefore Banach, and $\mu(E)=1$. The same map $W$ is Borel as an $E$-valued map because the Borel sets of $E$ are intersections of $E$ with Borel sets of $B$. For any $\ell\in E^*$, let $p(x)=\|\ell\|_{E^*}\|x\|_B$ on $B$; $\ell$ is dominated by $p$ on $E$. By [A2] it extends to a linear $\widetilde\ell$ on $B$ dominated by $p$, and applying domination to $x$ and $-x$ gives $|\widetilde\ell(x)|\le\|\ell\|_{E^*}\|x\|_B$. Since $W\in E$ almost surely, $\ell(W)=\widetilde\ell(W)$ almost surely, so $\ell(W)$ is centered normal. Thus the restricted law is Gaussian.

For tightness in $E$, replace each compact $K_m$ by $K_m\cap E$, which is compact and has the same $\mu$-mass because $\mu(E)=1$. If $x\notin E$, closedness gives a $B$-open neighborhood disjoint from $E$, of $\mu$-mass zero, so $x$ is outside the ambient support. If $x\in E$, every ambient open ball about $x$ intersects $E$ in an $E$-open neighborhood and has the same measure as that intersection; hence all such neighborhoods have positive measure exactly when all relative neighborhoods do. The two supports therefore agree.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let $p,q:\mathsf X\to[0,\infty)$ be measurable densities with $\int p\,d\mu=\int q\,d\mu=1$. They define probability laws $P(B)=\int_Bp\,d\mu$ and $Q(B)=\int_Bq\,d\mu$ ([[def-probability-measure]]). Their **root-L2 Hellinger distance**, with the root-L2 normalization, is
$$h(P,Q):=\left(\int_{\mathsf X}(\sqrt p-\sqrt q)^2\,d\mu\right)^{1/2}.$$

The dominating measure $\mu$ is fixed throughout a use of this definition. Changing either density on a $\mu$-null set does not change the value, since the integrand changes only on a null set. This definition does not assert that separate choices of density versions are jointly measurable in an additional parameter.

Let $n\in\mathbb N$, and suppose $f$ has derivatives through order $n+1$ on the closed interval between $a$ and $x$, with the usual endpoint continuity. If $|f^{(n+1)}(t)|\le M$ throughout that interval, then
$$|R_{n,a}f(x)|\le \frac{M}{\iota((n+1)!)}|x-a|^{n+1}.$$

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$ be a
limit point of $A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]). If $f$ is differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) then $f$ is continuous at $c$ ([[def-continuity-real]]).

Consequently, if $f$ is differentiable on a set $S \subseteq A$ then $f$ is
continuous at every point of $S$.

**No converse is asserted, and none holds.** Continuity at $c$ does not give
differentiability at $c$, and the standard witness is worked out on the
companion page.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.

isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts

and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

derivations.claim: For each $x$, [F1] gives $|\Psi(w(x))-\Psi(w_0(x))|\le L|w(x)-w_0(x)|$. The two values of $y$ contribute the same squared difference to $d_2^2$, so integration gives $d_2^2=2\int|\Psi(w)-\Psi(w_0)|^2dG\le2L^2\|w-w_0\|_2^2$.

Fix $x$ and write $u_0=w_0(x)$. The Bernoulli directional divergence at $x$ is $k_x(u)=\Psi(u_0)\log\frac{\Psi(u_0)}{\Psi(u)}+(1-\Psi(u_0))\log\frac{1-\Psi(u_0)}{1-\Psi(u)}.$ By [F2] and the chain rule, $k_x'(u)=\frac{\Psi'(u)}{\Psi(u)(1-\Psi(u))}(\Psi(u)-\Psi(u_0))$. Thus $|k_x'(u)|\le RL|u-u_0|$ by [F1], and integration from $u_0$ to $w(x)$ yields $|k_x(w(x))|\le(RL/2)|w(x)-w_0(x)|^2$. Integrating over $G$ and using $\mathrm{KL}(Q_{w_0}\Vert Q_w)=\int k_x(w(x))\,G(dx)$ proves the stated upper bound.

The derivatives in [F2] have absolute values at most $R$: indeed $\Psi'/\Psi=(\Psi'/[\Psi(1-\Psi)])(1-\Psi)$ and $\Psi'/(1-\Psi)=(\Psi'/[\Psi(1-\Psi)])\Psi$. The mean-value theorem therefore bounds both Bernoulli log-probability ratios at $x$ by $R|w(x)-w_0(x)|$. Their squared conditional average under $Y|X=x\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(\Psi(w_0(x)))$ is at most $R^2|w(x)-w_0(x)|^2$; integrating over $G$ proves the log-square bound.

Let $P,Q$ be probability measures on the same measurable space
([[def-probability-measure]]). Absolute continuity $P\ll Q$ has the convention
of [[def-absolutely-continuous-with-respect-to-a-positive-measure]]. If
$P\not\ll Q$, define $D(P\|Q)=+\infty$. If $P\ll Q$, assume AC
([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) as in [[def-likelihood-ratio-as-rn-derivative]] and
let $r=dP/dQ$ be a finite-valued nonnegative measurable representative of its
Radon–Nikodym class; such a representative exists by
[[lem-radon-nikodym-density-of-a-finite-positive-measure-has-a-nonnegative-representative]].
On $\{r=0\}$ set $\ell=0$, and on $\{r>0\}$ set $\ell=\log r$. This
function is measurable: for $a\ge0$, $\{\ell>a\}=\{r>\exp(a)\}$, and for
$a<0$, $\{\ell>a\}=\{r=0\}\cup\{r>\exp(a)\}$, by the inverse and
monotonicity properties of the natural logarithm
([[def-natural-logarithm]], [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]]). These are
measurable sets by [[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]. Since
$P(\{r=0\})=\int_{\{r=0\}}r\,dQ=0$ by
[[thm-likelihood-ratio-change-of-measure]], the value chosen there does not
affect $\int\ell\,dP$. Define
$$D(P\|Q):=\int \ell\,dP,$$
where $\log$ is the natural logarithm ([[def-natural-logarithm]]).

The definition is independent of the representative: two representatives
agree $Q$-almost everywhere, hence $P$-almost everywhere. Put
$$\psi(0):=0,\qquad \psi(t):=t\log t\quad(t>0).$$
The function $\psi$ is continuous at zero: for $s\ge1$,
$$0\le \frac{\log s}{s}=\frac1s\int_1^s\frac{du}{u}\le\frac1s\int_1^s\frac{du}{\sqrt u}\le\frac2{\sqrt s}.$$
Thus $t\log t\to0$ as $t\downarrow0$; here $L=\log$ by
[[cor-integral-logarithm-agrees-with-natural-logarithm]] and
[[def-integral-logarithm]]. On $(0,\infty)$, $\psi$ is a product of continuous
functions by [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]] and
[[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]], so $\psi$ is continuous on
$[0,\infty)$ and $\psi(r)$ is measurable by
[[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]. Its signed integral is
defined by the positive and negative parts
([[def-positive-and-negative-parts-of-a-function]],
[[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]]).

For $0<t\le1$, the function $-t\log t$ has derivative $-\log t-1$ and
maximum $1/e$ at $t=1/e$: $e=\exp(1)>1$ by
[[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]] and
[[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]], $1/e=\exp(-1)$ by
[[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], and $\log(1/e)=-1$ by
[[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]] and the inverse definition. The mean value
theorem gives increase before and decrease after this point
([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[thm-integral-logarithm-derivative-and-normalisation]],
[[cor-integral-logarithm-agrees-with-natural-logarithm]], [[cor-mean-value-theorem]]).
At $t=0$ the negative part is zero. Since $Q$ is a probability measure,
$$\int \psi(r)^-\,dQ\le\frac1e.$$
The change-of-measure identity of [[thm-likelihood-ratio-change-of-measure]],
applied to $\ell^-$ gives $\int\ell^-\,dP=\int\psi(r)^-\,dQ\le1/e$,
so $\int\ell\,dP$ is well-defined; applying it to both positive and negative
parts gives
$$D(P\|Q)=\int\ell\,dP=\int\psi(r)\,dQ=\int r\log r\,dQ,$$
with $0\log0:=0$ and a finite negative part. Therefore the extended integral
is well-defined without an $\infty-\infty$ ambiguity.

This convention is directional: the first argument must be absolutely
continuous with respect to the second for the integral formula to apply.

Assume AC. Define $\gamma(E)=\int_E e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,dx$ for Borel E in $\mathbb R$. By [[lem-normal-density-has-total-mass-one]] and [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]], gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. [[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]] makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in [[def-dirac-measure]].

Assume the Axiom of Choice. If $0\le s,t$ and a real random variable
$X_t-X_s$ has law $N(0,|t-s|)$, then, for every integer $m\ge1$,
$$E|X_t-X_s|^{2m}=c_m|t-s|^m,$$
where
$$c_m=E|Z|^{2m}=(2m-1)!!=1\cdot3\cdots(2m-1)<\infty$$
for $Z\sim N(0,1)$. In particular, when $m\ge2$, this is the moment hypothesis
of the one-parameter Kolmogorov criterion with
$\alpha=2m$, $\beta=m-1$, and $C_T=c_m$.

derivations.claim: Put $e_i=Y_i-w_0(x_i)$ and $\delta_i=w(x_i)-w_0(x_i)$. Direct substitution of the normal densities from [F1] gives $\log\frac{p_i(Y_i)}{p_{i0}(Y_i)}=\log\frac{\sigma_0}{\sigma}-\frac{(e_i-\delta_i)^2}{2\sigma^2}+\frac{e_i^2}{2\sigma_0^2}.$ Taking its negative expectation and using [F2] yields $K_i:=\mathrm{KL}(P_{i0}\Vert P_i)=\log\frac{\sigma}{\sigma_0}+\frac{\sigma_0^2+\delta_i^2}{2\sigma^2}-\frac12.$

Let $s=\sigma-\sigma_0$ and $g(\sigma)=\log(\sigma/\sigma_0)+\sigma_0^2/(2\sigma^2)-1/2$. Then $g(\sigma_0)=g'(\sigma_0)=0$. Its second derivative is bounded uniformly when $\sigma,\sigma_0\in[a,b]$, so [F3] gives $|g(\sigma)|\le C_{a,b}s^2$. Explicitly, $g'(\sigma)=1/\sigma-\sigma_0^2/\sigma^3$ vanishes at $\sigma_0$, and $|g''(\sigma)|=|-1/\sigma^2+3\sigma_0^2/\sigma^4|\le a^{-2}+3b^2a^{-4}$. Also $\delta_i^2/(2\sigma^2)\le\delta_i^2/(2a^2)$. The formula in step 1.1 therefore gives $|K_i|\le C_{a,b}(\delta_i^2+s^2)$ and, in particular, the first claimed upper bound after averaging.

The log ratio in step 1.1 equals $m_i+B_i e_i+A(e_i^2-\sigma_0^2)$, where $A=1/(2\sigma_0^2)-1/(2\sigma^2)$, $B_i=\delta_i/\sigma^2$, and $m_i=-K_i$. On $[a,b]$, $|A|\le C_{a,b}|s|$ and $|B_i|\le a^{-2}|\delta_i|$. By [F2], $E e_i^2=\sigma_0^2$, $E(e_i^2-\sigma_0^2)^2=2\sigma_0^4$, and $E[e_i(e_i^2-\sigma_0^2)]=0$. Therefore the second moment is $K_i^2+B_i^2\sigma_0^2+2A^2\sigma_0^4$. Step 2.1 gives $K_i^2\le C_{a,b}(\delta_i^2+s^2)^2$, which is at most a constant times $\delta_i^2+s^2$ under the local bounds. Averaging proves the log-square inequality.

Let $n\ge1$, let $X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}$ be independent real random variables on a
common probability space, and let $g_i:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be Borel
measurable for each $i<n$.

1. If every $g_i$ is nonnegative, then
   $$\mathbb E\left[\prod_{i<n}g_i(X_i)\right]=\prod_{i<n}\mathbb E[g_i(X_i)]$$
   in $[0,+\infty]$. In this finite product of expectations, a zero factor
   makes the product zero even when another factor is $+\infty$; otherwise
   multiplication has its usual extended nonnegative meaning.
2. If every $g_i(X_i)$ is integrable, then $\prod_{i<n}g_i(X_i)$ is integrable
   and the same factorization holds in $\mathbb R$.

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]) and let $T : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n$ be linear
with matrix $A$ ([[def-linear-map]],
[[lem-euclidean-linear-maps-have-matrices-and-are-bounded]]).

1. **Invertible case.** If $\det A \ne 0$, then $T[E]$ is Lebesgue measurable for
   every Lebesgue measurable $E$ and
   $$\lambda_n\big(T[E]\big) \;=\; |\det A|\;\lambda_n(E),$$
   both sides possibly $+\infty$; the product is defined in
   $\overline{\mathbb{R}}$ because $|\det A| > 0$.
2. **Singular case.** If $\det A = 0$, then $T[E]$ is Lebesgue measurable with

**The singular clause is stated as nullity and not as a product.** When

Exponential Markov and step 1.2 give the upper tail $\exp(-nt^2/(4V_b))$; applying the same argument to the negative centered sum gives the lower tail. Adding the two bounds proves the claimed quadratic-statistic inequality.

Let $P,Q$ be probability measures on the same measurable space
([[def-probability-measure]]). Absolute continuity $P\ll Q$ has the convention
of [[def-absolutely-continuous-with-respect-to-a-positive-measure]]. If
$P\not\ll Q$, define $D(P\|Q)=+\infty$. If $P\ll Q$, assume AC
([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) as in [[def-likelihood-ratio-as-rn-derivative]] and
let $r=dP/dQ$ be a finite-valued nonnegative measurable representative of its
Radon–Nikodym class; such a representative exists by
[[lem-radon-nikodym-density-of-a-finite-positive-measure-has-a-nonnegative-representative]].
On $\{r=0\}$ set $\ell=0$, and on $\{r>0\}$ set $\ell=\log r$. This
function is measurable: for $a\ge0$, $\{\ell>a\}=\{r>\exp(a)\}$, and for
$a<0$, $\{\ell>a\}=\{r=0\}\cup\{r>\exp(a)\}$, by the inverse and
monotonicity properties of the natural logarithm
([[def-natural-logarithm]], [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]]). These are
measurable sets by [[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]. Since
$P(\{r=0\})=\int_{\{r=0\}}r\,dQ=0$ by
[[thm-likelihood-ratio-change-of-measure]], the value chosen there does not
affect $\int\ell\,dP$. Define
$$D(P\|Q):=\int \ell\,dP,$$
where $\log$ is the natural logarithm ([[def-natural-logarithm]]).

The definition is independent of the representative: two representatives
agree $Q$-almost everywhere, hence $P$-almost everywhere. Put
$$\psi(0):=0,\qquad \psi(t):=t\log t\quad(t>0).$$
The function $\psi$ is continuous at zero: for $s\ge1$,
$$0\le \frac{\log s}{s}=\frac1s\int_1^s\frac{du}{u}\le\frac1s\int_1^s\frac{du}{\sqrt u}\le\frac2{\sqrt s}.$$
Thus $t\log t\to0$ as $t\downarrow0$; here $L=\log$ by
[[cor-integral-logarithm-agrees-with-natural-logarithm]] and
[[def-integral-logarithm]]. On $(0,\infty)$, $\psi$ is a product of continuous
functions by [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]] and
[[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]], so $\psi$ is continuous on
$[0,\infty)$ and $\psi(r)$ is measurable by
[[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]. Its signed integral is
defined by the positive and negative parts
([[def-positive-and-negative-parts-of-a-function]],
[[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]]).

For $0<t\le1$, the function $-t\log t$ has derivative $-\log t-1$ and
maximum $1/e$ at $t=1/e$: $e=\exp(1)>1$ by
[[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]] and
[[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]], $1/e=\exp(-1)$ by
[[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], and $\log(1/e)=-1$ by
[[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]] and the inverse definition. The mean value
theorem gives increase before and decrease after this point
([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[thm-integral-logarithm-derivative-and-normalisation]],
[[cor-integral-logarithm-agrees-with-natural-logarithm]], [[cor-mean-value-theorem]]).
At $t=0$ the negative part is zero. Since $Q$ is a probability measure,
$$\int \psi(r)^-\,dQ\le\frac1e.$$
The change-of-measure identity of [[thm-likelihood-ratio-change-of-measure]],
applied to $\ell^-$ gives $\int\ell^-\,dP=\int\psi(r)^-\,dQ\le1/e$,
so $\int\ell\,dP$ is well-defined; applying it to both positive and negative
parts gives
$$D(P\|Q)=\int\ell\,dP=\int\psi(r)\,dQ=\int r\log r\,dQ,$$
with $0\log0:=0$ and a finite negative part. Therefore the extended integral
is well-defined without an $\infty-\infty$ ambiguity.

This convention is directional: the first argument must be absolutely
continuous with respect to the second for the integral formula to apply.

Let $X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ be random elements on a
common probability space. For each $i$, write

$$\sigma(X_i):=\{X_i^{-1}(B):B\in\Sigma_i\}\subseteq\mathcal F.$$

The family $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ is **independent** when the sigma-algebras
$(\sigma(X_i))_{i\in I}$ are independent in the sense of
[[def-independent-sigma-algebras-and-events]].

When $\Sigma_i$ is a Borel sigma-algebra, this agrees with the notation
$\sigma(X_i)$ from [[def-sigma-algebra-generated-by-a-function]].

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be an independent family of random elements
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$. For each $i$, let
$g_i:(S_i,\Sigma_i)\to(T_i,\mathcal T_i)$ be measurable. Then the family
$(g_i\circ X_i)_{i\in I}$ is independent.

Let $n\ge1$, let $X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}$ be independent real random variables on a
common probability space, and let $g_i:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be Borel
measurable for each $i<n$.

1. If every $g_i$ is nonnegative, then
   $$\mathbb E\left[\prod_{i<n}g_i(X_i)\right]=\prod_{i<n}\mathbb E[g_i(X_i)]$$
   in $[0,+\infty]$. In this finite product of expectations, a zero factor
   makes the product zero even when another factor is $+\infty$; otherwise
   multiplication has its usual extended nonnegative meaning.
2. If every $g_i(X_i)$ is integrable, then $\prod_{i<n}g_i(X_i)$ is integrable
   and the same factorization holds in $\mathbb R$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space, let $f\in L^1(\mathbb P)$
be real-valued, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval containing $f(x)$ for
almost every $x$, and let $\varphi:I\to\mathbb R$ be convex with
$\varphi\circ f\in L^1(\mathbb P)$. Then
$$\varphi\!\left(\int f\,d\mathbb P\right)\le\int\varphi(f)\,d\mathbb P.$$

For a finite family $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ of square-integrable real random variables on one common probability space,
$$\operatorname{Var}\!\left(\sum_{i\in I}X_i\right)=\sum_{i\in I}\operatorname{Var}(X_i)+2\sum_{\{i,j\}\subseteq I}\operatorname{Cov}(X_i,X_j).$$
Equivalently, it is $\sum_{i,j\in I}\operatorname{Cov}(X_i,X_j)$. The empty sum has variance zero, and the singleton formula is the identity.
The original finite-probability-space case is included, since every real random variable there is square-integrable and the covariance/variance definitions agree with the finite centered-product/square formulas.
In the first display, the second sum is over two-element subsets of $I$.

If $X$ is a square-integrable real random variable and $a>0$, then
$$\mathbb P(|X-\mathbb E[X]|\ge a)\le\frac{\operatorname{Var}(X)}{a^2}.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

For fixed $\theta$, independence [F1]–[F2] gives $E_0R_n(\theta)=\prod_i\int_{\{p_{i0}>0\}}p_{i\theta}\,d\mu_i\le1.$ Tonelli [F6] then gives $E_0D_n\le1$, so $D_n<\infty$ almost surely.

Let $\Pi_{K_n}$ be $\Pi$ conditioned on $K_n$ and set $Z_n=\int_{K_n}\sum_i\log\frac{p_{i\theta}(Y_i)}{p_{i0}(Y_i)}\,\Pi_{K_n}(d\theta).$ The finite local second moments make these integrals square-integrable. Jensen [F3] applied to the conditional prior integral yields $E_0V_i(Y_i)^2\le\int_{K_n}E_{i0}\!\left[\log\frac{p_{i\theta}(Y_i)}{p_{i0}(Y_i)}\right]^2\Pi_{K_n}(d\theta),$ so $\operatorname{Var}_0 Z_n\le n\epsilon_n^2$.

Jensen for $\log$ gives $D_n\ge\int_{K_n}R_n(\theta)\Pi(d\theta)\ge\Pi(K_n)\exp(Z_n).$ On the complementary event, this is at least $e^{-(C+2)n\epsilon_n^2}$. Together with step 1.1 this proves the claim.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. Let $Z_1,\ldots,Z_n$ be independent $N(0,1)$ variables, let $c_1,\ldots,c_n,\delta_1,\ldots,\delta_n\in\mathbb R$, and let $0<\sigma\le b$. Put $\|c\|_n^2=n^{-1}\sum_i c_i^2$ and $\|\delta\|_n^2=n^{-1}\sum_i\delta_i^2$. For $t>0$,
$$\Pr\!\left(\left|n^{-1}\sum_i c_i\sigma Z_i\right|\ge t\right)\le2\exp\!\left(-\frac{nt^2}{2\sigma^2\|c\|_n^2}\right),$$
with zero probability when $\|c\|_n=0$. If $\|\delta\|_n\le1$ and $0<t\le b^2+2$, then
$$\Pr\!\left(\left|n^{-1}\sum_i(\delta_i+\sigma Z_i)^2-(\sigma^2+\|\delta\|_n^2)\right|\ge t\right)\le2\exp\!\left(-\frac{nt^2}{4V_b}\right),\qquad V_b=2b^4+4b^2.$$

Under the truth, $U_j$ is centered normal with variance $\sigma_0^2\rho_j^2/n$, so [F1] gives $P_0^n(\phi_j=1)\le\exp[-n\rho_j^2/(32b^2)]$.

For an upper scale alternative, this mean is at least $\sigma_0^2+aM\epsilon_n$; for a lower scale alternative, it is at most $\sigma_0^2-aM\epsilon_n+\Delta^2\le\sigma_0^2-aM\epsilon_n/2$ once $M\epsilon_n\le2a$. Define $\phi_+=\mathbf1\{Q_n\ge\sigma_0^2+aM\epsilon_n/4\}$ and $\phi_-=\mathbf1\{Q_n\le\sigma_0^2-aM\epsilon_n/4\}$. Under the truth and on this scale-alternative region, the relevant deviations from the respective means are at least $aM\epsilon_n/4$.

Assume AC and countable choice. Let $\mu$ be a centered tight Borel Gaussian
law on a real separable Banach
space $B$, and let $H\subseteq B$ be its covariance RKHS. Define
$\operatorname{supp}\mu$ to be the set of $x\in B$ for which every open
neighborhood has positive $\mu$-measure. Then
$$\operatorname{supp}\mu=\overline H^{\,B}.$$

Assume AC and countable choice. Let $\mu$ be a centered tight Borel Gaussian law on a real separable Banach
space $B$, with covariance RKHS $H$, and let $w_0\in\overline H^{\,B}$. For
$\varepsilon>0$, write
$\varepsilon B^\circ=\{x\in B:\|x\|_B<\varepsilon\}$ and define the
**concentration function**
$$\phi_{w_0}(\varepsilon) =\inf_{\substack{h\in H\\\|h-w_0\|_B<\varepsilon}} \left\{\|h\|_H^2-\log\mu(\varepsilon B^\circ)\right\}.$$
The feasible set is nonempty because $w_0$ lies in the Banach-norm closure of
$H$. Also $\mu(\varepsilon B^\circ)>0$ because $0\in\operatorname{supp}\mu$;
thus the logarithm is finite. The value is finite and nonnegative. The support assertion used here is
[[thm-support-of-banach-gaussian-is-closure-of-rkhs]].

Assume AC and countable choice. Let $\mu$ be a centered tight Borel Gaussian
law on a real separable Banach
space $B$, with covariance RKHS $H$, and let $w_0\in\overline H^{\,B}$.
Suppose $n\ge1$, $\varepsilon>0$, $C>1$,
$e^{-Cn\varepsilon^2}<1/2$, and
$\phi_{w_0}(\varepsilon)\le n\varepsilon^2$, where $\phi_{w_0}$ is the
concentration function. Then there is a measurable set $B_n\subseteq B$
such that
$$\log N(3\varepsilon,B_n,\|\cdot\|_B)\le6Cn\varepsilon^2,\qquad \mu(B\setminus B_n)\le e^{-Cn\varepsilon^2},$$
and
$$\mu\{\|W-w_0\|_B<2\varepsilon\}\ge e^{-n\varepsilon^2}.$$

contraction without separate statistical-distance and Kullback–Leibler
comparisons.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ be a probability space and let $B$ be a real
separable Banach space with its norm Borel sigma-algebra. A map
$W:\Omega\to B$ is a **centered Borel Gaussian random element** if it is
Borel-measurable and, for every $\ell\in B^*$, the real random variable
$\ell(W)$ has a centered (possibly zero-variance) normal law. Its law is the
Borel probability $\mu=P\circ W^{-1}$. When the word *tight* is used, it means
that for every $\delta>0$ there is a norm-compact $K\subseteq B$ with
$\mu(K)>1-\delta$.

This definition concerns a random element in $B$. A Gaussian process on an
arbitrary index set with only a cylinder-space law does not satisfy it unless
a Borel $B$-valued realization is separately constructed.

Assume AC. Let $W$ be a centered Borel Gaussian random element in a real separable
Banach space $B$, with law $\mu$. For $\ell\in B^*$ define
$$C\ell=E[\ell(W)W]\in B,\qquad Q(\ell,m)=E[\ell(W)m(W)]\quad(\ell,m\in B^*).$$
The **Cameron–Martin reproducing-kernel Hilbert space** $H$ is the completion
of $B^*/N$ in the inner product induced by $Q$, where
$N=\{\ell\in B^*:Q(\ell,\ell)=0\}$. The canonical map sends the class of
$\ell$ to $C\ell$ and extends continuously to an injective map $i:H\to B$;
we identify $H$ with its image in $B$ and use the completed Hilbert norm
$\|\cdot\|_H$. The preceding construction is well-defined by
[[thm-banach-gaussian-covariance-rkhs-is-well-defined]].

The term *RKHS* here denotes this covariance-induced Hilbert space of shifts
inside $B$; it is not the space of all continuous functions on an arbitrary
index set.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Work over ZF. The **real dominated-extension principle**, denoted **HB**, is the following assertion:

For every real vector space $X$, every sublinear functional $p:X\to\mathbb R$ in the sense of [[def-sublinear-functional]], every real linear subspace $M\le X$ in the sense of [[def-linear-subspace]], and every real linear functional $g:M\to\mathbb R$ in the sense of [[def-algebraic-dual-and-linear-functional]],
$$\bigl(\forall m\in M,\ g(m)\le p(m)\bigr)\ \Longrightarrow\ \exists F:X\to\mathbb R\ \bigl(F\text{ is real linear},\ F|_M=g,\ \forall x\in X,\ F(x)\le p(x)\bigr).$$

This names an additional principle; it does not assert a proof of HB in ZF. Subsequent results explicitly state when they assume HB. Neither topology nor completeness is part of this assertion. The subspace may be $\{0\}$ or all of $X$. Sublinearity at scalar zero gives $p(0)=0$, and a linear functional has value zero at zero.

Let $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ be a measurable parameter space, $\Pi$ a prior probability measure on it, and $p_\theta$ a jointly measurable family of finite-valued probability densities relative to one fixed sigma-finite measure $\mu$. Let $P_0$ have finite-valued density $p_0$ relative to $\mu$, and let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be IID with law $P_0$. Assume the Axiom of Choice for the imported directional KL convention ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). The jointly measurable density family is explicit input, so no arbitrary-index selection of versions is used here. In the expression below, the weighted log terms are set to zero on $\{p_0=0\}$; on $\{p_0>0,p_\theta=0\}$ the log ratio is $-\infty$ and its square is $+\infty$. For $\epsilon_n>0$, define
$$K_n:=\left\{\theta:\mathrm{KL}(P_0\Vert P_\theta)\le\epsilon_n^2,\quad \int\left[\log\frac{p_\theta}{p_0}\right]^2p_0\,d\mu\le\epsilon_n^2\right\}.$$
Joint measurability and Tonelli make $K_n$ measurable, as verified below. If $\Pi(K_n)\ge e^{-Cn\epsilon_n^2}$ for $C>0$ and $\mathrm{KL}(P_0\Vert P_\theta)$ uses the direction in [[def-kullback-leibler-divergence]], then, defining the ratio to be zero on the $P_0$-null set where $p_0=0$, the likelihood denominator
$$D_n:=\int_\Theta\prod_{i=1}^n\frac{p_\theta(X_i)}{p_0(X_i)}\,\Pi(d\theta)$$
is finite and positive $P_0^n$-almost surely and
$$P_0^n\!\left\{D_n\ge e^{-(C+2)n\epsilon_n^2}\right\}\ge1-\frac1{n\epsilon_n^2}.$$

Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space with a fixed sigma-finite measure. A probability density is a finite-valued nonnegative measurable $p$ with $\int p\,d\mu=1$, and its induced law is $P_p=p\,d\mu$ as in [[def-measure-with-density]]. Let $p_0$ be a probability density and write $P_0:=p_0\,d\mu$. Let $\mathcal F$ be a family of such densities, write $P_p:=p\,d\mu$ for $p\in\mathcal F$, and let $\mathcal F_n\subseteq\mathcal F$ be nonempty. Let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be IID under each law used below. The selected metric $d$ is one of:

- the root-L2 Hellinger distance $h$ of [[def-hellinger-distance-between-density-laws]];
- the full density distance $d_1(p,q):=\int|p-q|\,d\mu$;
- the density distance $d_2(p,q):=(\int|p-q|^2\,d\mu)^{1/2}$, provided a fixed $B>0$ bounds $p_0$ and every $p\in\mathcal F$ by $B$ almost everywhere.

For $r>0$, let $D(r,\mathcal F_n,d)$ be the supremum of the cardinalities of finite subsets of $\mathcal F_n$ whose distinct points have $d$-distance greater than $r$. Suppose $\epsilon_n>0$, $\epsilon_n\to0$, $n\epsilon_n^2\to\infty$, and
$$\log D(\epsilon_n,\mathcal F_n,d)\le n\epsilon_n^2.$$
Then for every fixed $M\ge128$ and all sufficiently large $n$, there is a measurable test $\phi_n:\mathsf X^n\to\{0,1\}$ such that, for some $c_d>0$ depending only on the selected metric (and on $B$ in the $d_2$ case),
$$P_0^n(\phi_n=1)\le2e^{-(c_dM^2-1)n\epsilon_n^2},$$
and $P_p^n(\phi_n=0)\le e^{-c_dM^2n\epsilon_n^2}$ for every $p\in\mathcal F_n$ with $d(p,p_0)>M\epsilon_n$.

The entropy metric is the same metric used in the separation and test-error conclusion. The $d_1$ convention is the full integral $\int|p-q|\,d\mu$, which equals twice the library event-supremum total variation distance.

Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal A,
u)$ be a measure space, and let $w,w_0:\mathsf X	o\mathbb R$ be measurable with finite positive normalizers $Z_w=\int e^w\,d
u$ and $Z_0=\int e^{w_0}\,d
u$. Set $p_w=e^w/Z_w$, $p_0=e^{w_0}/Z_0$, and $r=\|w-w_0\|_\infty\le1$. With root-L2 Hellinger distance as in [[def-hellinger-distance-between-density-laws]], and the directional convention of [[def-kullback-leibler-divergence]],
$$h(P_w,P_0)\le e^r r,\qquad \mathrm{KL}(P_0\Vert P_w)\le 	frac12 e^{2r}r^2,\qquad \int\left(\log rac{p_w}{p_0}ight)^2p_0\,d
u\le4r^2.$$

Let $G$ be a probability measure on $(\mathsf X,\mathcal A)$, let $\Psi:\mathbb R\to(0,1)$ be differentiable, and suppose
$$L:=\sup_{u\in\mathbb R}|\Psi'(u)|<\infty,\qquad R:=\sup_{u\in\mathbb R}\left|\frac{\Psi'(u)}{\Psi(u)(1-\Psi(u))}\right|<\infty.$$
For measurable real functions $w,w_0$, define Bernoulli densities relative to $G\otimes\#$, where $\#$ is counting measure on $\{0,1\}$, by
$$q_w(x,y)=\Psi(w(x))^y(1-\Psi(w(x)))^{1-y},\qquad q_{w_0}(x,y)=\Psi(w_0(x))^y(1-\Psi(w_0(x)))^{1-y}.$$
If $w-w_0\in L^2(G)$, then, with $d_2(q_w,q_{w_0})^2=\int|q_w-q_{w_0}|^2\,d(G\otimes\#)$,
$$d_2(q_w,q_{w_0})^2\le2L^2\|w-w_0\|_{L^2(G)}^2,$$
$$\mathrm{KL}(Q_{w_0}\Vert Q_w)\le\frac{LR}{2}\|w-w_0\|_{L^2(G)}^2,\qquad E_{Q_{w_0}}\!\left[\left(\log\frac{q_w(X,Y)}{q_{w_0}(X,Y)}\right)^2\right]\le R^2\|w-w_0\|_{L^2(G)}^2.$$

Let $0<a<b<\infty$, let $\sigma_0,\sigma\in[a,b]$, and fix design points $x_1,\ldots,x_n$. Under the true independent laws $Y_i\sim N(w_0(x_i),\sigma_0^2)$, the model has independent laws $Y_i\sim N(w(x_i),\sigma^2)$. Write $\delta_i=w(x_i)-w_0(x_i)$ and $\|\delta\|_n^2=n^{-1}\sum_i\delta_i^2$. There is a finite constant $C_{a,b}$, depending only on $a,b$, such that whenever $\max_i|\delta_i|\le1$ and $|\sigma-\sigma_0|\le1$,
$$\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\mathrm{KL}(P_{i0}\Vert P_i)\le C_{a,b}(\|\delta\|_n^2+|\sigma-\sigma_0|^2),$$
$$\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n E_{i0}\!\left[\left(\log\frac{p_i(Y_i)}{p_{i0}(Y_i)}\right)^2\right]\le C_{a,b}(\|\delta\|_n^2+|\sigma-\sigma_0|^2).$$

Assume AC. For each $n$, let $Y_1,\ldots,Y_n$ be independent, with true densities $p_{i0}$ and candidate densities $p_{i\theta}$ relative to supplied sigma-finite measures $\mu_i$. Assume $(\theta,y)\mapsto p_{i\theta}(y)$ is jointly measurable and let $\Pi$ be a prior. If a measurable set $K_n$ satisfies
$$\Pi(K_n)\ge e^{-Cn\epsilon_n^2},\quad \sup_{\theta\in K_n}\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\mathrm{KL}(P_{i0}\Vert P_{i\theta})\le\epsilon_n^2,\quad \sup_{\theta\in K_n}\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n E_{i0}\!\left[\log\frac{p_{i\theta}(Y_i)}{p_{i0}(Y_i)}\right]^2\le\epsilon_n^2,$$
then the denominator
$$D_n=\int\prod_{i=1}^n\frac{p_{i\theta}(Y_i)}{p_{i0}(Y_i)}\,\Pi(d\theta)$$
is finite $P_0^{(n)}$-almost surely and satisfies
$$P_0^{(n)}\{D_n\ge e^{-(C+2)n\epsilon_n^2}\}\ge1-\frac1{n\epsilon_n^2}.$$

For each $n$, let $P_{\theta,n}$ and $P_{0,n}$ have jointly measurable densities $p_{\theta,n}$ and $p_{0,n}$ relative to a common sigma-finite measure, and let $\Pi$ be a prior. Let $\Theta_n$ be a measurable sieve, let
$$A_n=\{\theta:d_n(\theta,\theta_0)>r_n\},$$
and let $D_n=\int p_{\theta,n}(Y)/p_{0,n}(Y)\,\Pi(d\theta)$ be the likelihood-ratio denominator on the $P_{0,n}$-full set where $p_{0,n}(Y)>0$. Suppose $\epsilon_n>0$, $n\epsilon_n^2\to\infty$, and constants $A<B$, $T>A$ satisfy
$$P_{0,n}\{D_n<e^{-An\epsilon_n^2}\}\to0,\qquad \Pi(\Theta_n^c)\le e^{-Bn\epsilon_n^2},$$
and there are measurable tests $\phi_n$ with
$$P_{0,n}(\phi_n=1)\le e^{-Tn\epsilon_n^2},\qquad \sup_{\theta\in A_n\cap\Theta_n}P_{\theta,n}(\phi_n=0)\le e^{-Tn\epsilon_n^2}.$$
Then the posterior mass of $A_n$ tends to zero in $P_{0,n}$-probability.

Let $B$ be a real Banach space and let $W$ be a Borel measurable $B$-valued random element with tight law $\mu$. Tight means that for every $\eta>0$ some compact $K\subset B$ satisfies $\mu(K)>1-\eta$. Assume $W$ is centered Gaussian, meaning that every continuous real linear functional $\ell:B\to\mathbb R$ makes $\ell(W)$ a centered scalar normal random variable. Then there is a separable closed linear subspace $E\subset B$ with $\mu(E)=1$. The law of $W$ viewed as an $E$-valued random element is tight and centered Gaussian, and its support in $E$ is exactly the support of $\mu$ in $B$, viewed as a subset of $B$. In particular, every ambient support point belongs to $E$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $W$ be a centered Gaussian random element in a real normed space $B$. Let $\ell\in B^*$ satisfy $\operatorname{Var}(\ell(W))=\tau^2>0$, and let $\mathbb H$ be a Hilbert subspace of $B$ with nonnegative squared norm. For $w_0\in B$, define
$$\phi_{w_0}(\epsilon)=\inf_{\substack{h\in\mathbb H\\\|h-w_0\|_B<\epsilon}}\left\{\|h\|_{\mathbb H}^2\right\}-\log\Pr(\|W\|_B<\epsilon),$$
with $\inf\varnothing=+\infty$. Then for every $\epsilon>0$,
$$\phi_{w_0}(\epsilon)\ge \log(1/\epsilon)-C_\ell,\qquad C_\ell=\log\!\left(\frac{2\|\ell\|_{B^*}}{\sqrt{2\pi}\tau}\right).$$

Assume HB and countable choice. Let $B$ be a real separable Banach space. There is a sequence
$(\ell_j)_{j\ge1}\subseteq B^*$ with $\|\ell_j\|=1$ such that
$$\|x\|=\sup_{j\ge1}|\ell_j(x)|\qquad(x\in B).$$
If $B=\{0\}$, the conclusion is interpreted using the zero functional and the
supremum is $0$.

Let $x_1,\ldots,x_n$ be deterministic, $Y_i=w_0(x_i)+\sigma_0Z_i$ under the truth with independent $Z_i\sim N(0,1)$, and let candidate parameters be $(w,\sigma)$ with $\sigma\in[a,b]$, $0<a<b$, and $\sigma_0\in[a,b]$. Put $\|u\|_n^2=n^{-1}\sum_i u(x_i)^2$. Suppose $\epsilon_n\to0$, $n\epsilon_n^2\to\infty$, and a measurable function sieve $B_n$ has a finite supremum-norm cover of radius $3\epsilon_n$ with at most $\exp(6C n\epsilon_n^2)$ centers, for a fixed $C>0$. For every $T>0$, there is a sufficiently large fixed $M$ and a measurable test $\phi_n$ such that, for all sufficiently large $n$,
$$P_0^n(\phi_n=1)\le e^{-Tn\epsilon_n^2},\qquad \sup_{\substack{w\in B_n,\ \sigma\in[a,b]\\ \|w-w_0\|_n+|\sigma-\sigma_0|>M\epsilon_n}}P_{w,\sigma}^n(\phi_n=0)\le e^{-Tn\epsilon_n^2}.$$

Assume AC. Let $Z_1,\ldots,Z_n$ be independent $N(0,1)$ variables, let $c_1,\ldots,c_n,\delta_1,\ldots,\delta_n\in\mathbb R$, and let $0<\sigma\le b$. Put $\|c\|_n^2=n^{-1}\sum_i c_i^2$ and $\|\delta\|_n^2=n^{-1}\sum_i\delta_i^2$. For $t>0$,
$$\Pr\!\left(\left|n^{-1}\sum_i c_i\sigma Z_i\right|\ge t\right)\le2\exp\!\left(-\frac{nt^2}{2\sigma^2\|c\|_n^2}\right),$$
with zero probability when $\|c\|_n=0$. If $\|\delta\|_n\le1$ and $0<t\le b^2+2$, then
$$\Pr\!\left(\left|n^{-1}\sum_i(\delta_i+\sigma Z_i)^2-(\sigma^2+\|\delta\|_n^2)\right|\ge t\right)\le2\exp\!\left(-\frac{nt^2}{4V_b}\right),\qquad V_b=2b^4+4b^2.$$

derivations.claim: The separable-support reduction [F5] leaves the inherited norm, law and support point unchanged. For the first two branches use the rate $r_n=\epsilon_n$; for the universal fixed-design branch use $r_n=\rho_n$. The concentration function is nonincreasing in its radius, because its feasible RKHS approximation set grows and centered small-ball probabilities increase. Thus $\phi_{w_0}(r_n)\le\phi_{w_0}(\epsilon_n)\le n\epsilon_n^2\le nr_n^2$. Both choices satisfy $r_n\to0$ and $nr_n^2\to\infty$. By [F8], the support point lies in the RKHS closure.

In log-Gaussian density estimation, evaluation measurability and Tonelli [F6] make $w\mapsto Z_w$ measurable. On its full-prior positive-finite set, $(w,x)\mapsto e^{w(x)}/Z_w$ is a jointly measurable density family. The $2r_n$ supremum ball has directional KL at most $2e^{4r_n}r_n^2$ and log-square at most $16r_n^2$ by [F3]. Choose a fixed sufficiently large $k$. Its prior mass is at least $e^{-nr_n^2}$ by [F10], so [F1] at radius $kr_n$ gives a denominator at least $e^{-A nr_n^2}$ for fixed $A=1+2k^2$ except with probability tending to zero.

In binary regression, [F3] places the $2r_n$ prior ball in a directional KL/log-square set of radius $k^2r_n^2$ for a fixed sufficiently large $k$. Its mass is at least $e^{-nr_n^2}$ by [F10], so [F1] gives the same type of denominator bound. The joint Bernoulli densities relative to $G\otimes\#$ are bounded by one, as required for the density-$L^2$ tests in [F2].

For the universal fixed-design branch take $r_n=\rho_n$. On $\|w-w_0\|_\infty<2r_n$ and $|\sigma-\sigma_0|<r_n$, [F3] bounds average directional KL and log-square by $Kr_n^2$ for fixed $K$. Independence and [A2], together with [F10], give joint local prior mass at least $cr_ne^{-nr_n^2}$. Since $r_n\ge\sqrt{\log n/n}$, eventually $\log(1/r_n)\le\tfrac12\log n\le\tfrac12nr_n^2$; hence this mass is at least $e^{-C_0nr_n^2}$ for fixed $C_0$. The independent-observation denominator lemma in [F4] applies.

For each branch choose $C>1$ larger than its denominator exponent; eventually $e^{-Cnr_n^2}<1/2$. Apply the prior sieve theorem [F10] using step 1.1 to get measurable $B_n$ with entropy at radius $3r_n$ at most $6Cnr_n^2$ and tail at most $e^{-Cnr_n^2}$. The same theorem supplies the local prior mass used in steps 1.2–1.4.

In the density branch intersect $B_n$ with the measurable positive-finite-normalizer set, changing its prior tail by zero. From a radius-$3r_n$ cover, select a valid center for every cover ball meeting that intersection; finite selection doubles the radius to $6r_n$ without increasing the number. The pairwise norm comparison [F3] sends this to a Hellinger cover of radius at most $7r_n$ for large $n$. Thus any $14r_n$-separated set has size at most $e^{6Cnr_n^2}$. Taking packing radius at least $\max\{14,\sqrt{6C}\}r_n$, [F2] gives tests with null and uniform sieve alternative errors at most $e^{-Tnr_n^2}$ for any fixed desired $T>A$, by increasing the alternative multiple. The denominator and sieve tail now satisfy the posterior split in [F4], proving contraction in probability.

In binary regression the norm-ball and sieve cover map by [F3] to density-$L^2$ balls and covers of constant times $r_n$. Taking packing radius at least twice the cover radius and at least $\sqrt{6C}r_n$ gives packing entropy at most its squared radius times $n$. By [F2] and [F4], the tests, denominator and sieve tail prove contraction in probability. Since the joint Bernoulli densities satisfy $d_2(q_w,q_{w_0})=\sqrt2\|\Psi(w)-f_0\|_{L^2(G)}$, this is the stated binary distance.

In fixed-design regression take the product sieve $B_n\times[a,b]$. Its prior tail is at most $e^{-Cnr_n^2}$, and its function component has the radius-$3r_n$ cover from step 2.1. The local fixed-design testing lemma [F14] gives tests outside $\|w-w_0\|_n+|\sigma-\sigma_0|>Mr_n$ with errors at most $e^{-Tnr_n^2}$ for any fixed $T$ by choosing fixed $M$ large. Choose $T$ and $C$ above the denominator exponent in step 1.4. The posterior split [F4] proves the universal $\rho_n$ contraction in probability.

If the Gaussian law is not $\delta_0$, [F13] supplies a continuous linear functional with nonzero Gaussian variance. Indeed, otherwise every member of a countable norming family would vanish almost surely, forcing $\|W\|=0$ almost surely. By [F7] there is a fixed constant $D$ such that $\log(1/\epsilon_n)\le n\epsilon_n^2+D$. Put $t_n=n\epsilon_n^2\to\infty$; then $\log n=\log t_n+2\log(1/\epsilon_n)\le3t_n+2D$ eventually, since $\log t_n\le t_n$. Consequently $\rho_n\le C_1\epsilon_n$ for fixed $C_1$. The universal conclusion in step 3.3 therefore proves the sharper $\epsilon_n$ conclusion after enlarging $M$ by $C_1$.

Now suppose $W=0$ almost surely and its scale density $g$ is bounded above by $U<\infty$ on $|\sigma-\sigma_0|<\delta$ within $[a,b]$. The support assumption forces $w_0=0$. Put $S_n=\sum_iY_i^2$, $q=S_n/(n\sigma_0^2)$, and $L_n(\sigma)=(\sigma_0/\sigma)^n\exp[(1-\sigma_0^2/\sigma^2)S_n/(2\sigma_0^2)]$. On $E_R=\{|S_n-n\sigma_0^2|\le R\sqrt n\}$, write $z=(\sigma-\sigma_0)/\sigma_0$. Compactness of the positive scale interval and Taylor's formula give constants $c,C>0$ independent of $n,R$ with $$-Cn(\sigma-\sigma_0)^2-CR\sqrt n|\sigma-\sigma_0|\le\log L_n(\sigma)\le-cn(\sigma-\sigma_0)^2+CR\sqrt n|\sigma-\sigma_0|.$$ For verification, its deterministic part is $n[-\log(1+z)+(1-(1+z)^{-2})/2]$, negative away from zero, with second derivative $-2$ at zero; the remaining term is $(S_n-n\sigma_0^2)(1-(1+z)^{-2})/(2\sigma_0^2)$, bounded by $CR\sqrt n|z|$. The residual-energy tail in [F15] with zero mean shift gives $\limsup_nP_0(E_R^c)\le2e^{-c_0R^2}$ for fixed $R$.

On $E_R$ integrate the likelihood over $|\sigma-\sigma_0|\le1/\sqrt n$ within $[a,b]$. This interval has length at least $1/\sqrt n$ for large $n$, even at an endpoint; [A2] and step 4.2 bound its integral below by $c_R/\sqrt n$ for some $c_R>0$. On the local neighborhood where $g\le U$, substitute $u=\sqrt n(\sigma-\sigma_0)$ in the numerator outside $M\epsilon_n$. Dividing by that lower bound gives at most $C_R\int_{|u|>M\sqrt n\epsilon_n}e^{-cu^2+CR|u|}du\to0$, since $n\epsilon_n^2\to\infty$. Outside the local neighborhood, step 4.2 bounds $L_n$ by $e^{-c'n}$ for large $n$, whose integral against the entire probability prior is at most $e^{-c'n}$; after dividing by the denominator this also tends to zero. First let $n\to\infty$ and then $R\to\infty$. This proves the sharper degenerate-prior contraction in probability for every fixed $M>0$.

In each proved branch the posterior tail is a random variable $T_n\in[0,1]$ converging to zero in probability. For $\eta>0$, $ET_n\le\eta+P(T_n>\eta)$; first take the limit superior and then $\eta\downarrow0$. Thus all asserted expectation limits follow. The universal fixed-design rate requires no upper bound on the scale density; the sharper degenerate alternative uses only the explicitly local upper bound.

Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let $p,q:\mathsf X\to[0,\infty)$ be measurable densities with $\int p\,d\mu=\int q\,d\mu=1$. They define probability laws $P(B)=\int_Bp\,d\mu$ and $Q(B)=\int_Bq\,d\mu$ ([[def-probability-measure]]). Their **root-L2 Hellinger distance**, with the root-L2 normalization, is
$$h(P,Q):=\left(\int_{\mathsf X}(\sqrt p-\sqrt q)^2\,d\mu\right)^{1/2}.$$

The dominating measure $\mu$ is fixed throughout a use of this definition. Changing either density on a $\mu$-null set does not change the value, since the integrand changes only on a null set. This definition does not assert that separate choices of density versions are jointly measurable in an additional parameter.

By [[lem-normal-density-has-total-mass-one]] and [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]], gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. [[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]] makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in [[def-dirac-measure]].

Let $\epsilon_n>0$ satisfy $\epsilon_n\to0$ and $n\epsilon_n^2\to\infty$. For the centered tight Gaussian prior in each branch, let $\mu$ be its law and let $B$ be a separable closed Banach carrier with the norm inherited from that branch's stated function space, as supplied by [[lem-tight-borel-gaussian-law-has-separable-support]]. Write $\mathbb H$ for the covariance RKHS of $\mu$ on $B$, and define
$$\phi_{w_0}(\epsilon)=\inf_{\substack{h\in\mathbb H\\\|h-w_0\|_B<\epsilon}}\left\{\|h\|_{\mathbb H}^2-\log\mu(\epsilon B^\circ)\right\},\qquad \epsilon B^\circ=\{u\in B:\|u\|_B<\epsilon\}.$$

Let $r \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $r^k$ be the integer power ([[def-integer-power]]),
so that $r^0 = 1$ for every $r$, including $r = 0$.

1. If $|r| < 1$ then the series $\sum r^k$ converges ([[def-series]]) and
   $$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} r^{k} \;=\; \frac{1}{1-r} .$$
2. If $|r| \ge 1$ then $\sum r^k$ diverges.

The series starts at $k = 0$ and its first term is $r^0 = 1$; in particular
$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} 2^{-k} = 2$, while the series starting at $k = 1$ sums to
$1$. Which starting index is meant has to be said, and it is said here.

Assume AC. Let $Z_1,\ldots,Z_n$ be independent $N(0,1)$ variables, let $c_1,\ldots,c_n,\delta_1,\ldots,\delta_n\in\mathbb R$, and let $0<\sigma\le b$. Put $\|c\|_n^2=n^{-1}\sum_i c_i^2$ and $\|\delta\|_n^2=n^{-1}\sum_i\delta_i^2$. For $t>0$,
$$\Pr\!\left(\left|n^{-1}\sum_i c_i\sigma Z_i\right|\ge t\right)\le2\exp\!\left(-\frac{nt^2}{2\sigma^2\|c\|_n^2}\right),$$
with zero probability when $\|c\|_n=0$. If $\|\delta\|_n\le1$ and $0<t\le b^2+2$, then
$$\Pr\!\left(\left|n^{-1}\sum_i(\delta_i+\sigma Z_i)^2-(\sigma^2+\|\delta\|_n^2)\right|\ge t\right)\le2\exp\!\left(-\frac{nt^2}{4V_b}\right),\qquad V_b=2b^4+4b^2.$$

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.
